detail.title: Investigating Treatment Effect Heterogeneity in Reduced Drug Use: A Causal Forest Analysis of Substance Use Disorder Psychosocial Interventions
detail.abstract: This study examines heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) in substance use disorder (SUD) treatments, focusing on reduced use—a non-abstinence-based outcome increasingly recognized as clinically meaningful. We applied causal forest models to identify HTE across psychosocial interventions using data from seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in the National Institute on Drug Abuse Clinical Trials Network (N = 3,614). We estimated conditional average treatment effects (CATE) and evaluated the proportion of outcome variability explained by CATE. We also conducted omnibus tests, calibration statistics, and Rank-Weighted Average Treatment Effect (RATE) analysis. While overall evidence of HTE was modest, we observed consistent signals for the combined Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment / Screening, Assessment, and Referral (SBIRT/SAR) intervention compared to treatment as usual. The omnibus test statistic was 1.19 (SE = 0.42, p = 0.002), and the RATE estimate was 0.12 (p = 0.002), supporting HTE. No evidence of HTE was found for other interventions. This application highlights the utility of causal forests in detecting treatment-effect heterogeneity in psychosocial SUD interventions, particularly when evaluating non-abstinence-based outcomes. Findings suggest that individual baseline characteristics may explain variation in treatment response, underscoring the importance of identifying potential effect modifiers.

title: ScorecardBuilder: An Automated framework for Creating Self-Organizing Risk Models
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Alabama at Birmingham, , affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham and University of Alabama at Birmingham

detail.title: ScorecardBuilder: An Automated framework for Creating Self-Organizing Risk Models
detail.abstract: Interpretable risk models remain difficult to construct at scale, especially for large datasets common across diverse analytical settings. This work introduces an automated scorecard-building system that transforms structured data into interpretable, bounded integer scores for workflow-integrated applications or decision support tools. The pipeline combines elastic-net logistic regression, monotonic binning, weight-of-evidence encoding, and mixed-integer optimization to produce transparent, statistically constrained models without requiring specialized expertise. It handles missingness, enforces reproducible preprocessing, and generates audit-friendly artifacts that support regulatory review. Using retrospective clinical data, the system demonstrates a generalizable framework for interpretable predictive modeling and advances trustworthy, infrastructure-aware deployment for multipurpose use.

title: Dynamic Investment and Product Market Rivalry: The Network Q Model
affiliations: and Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Dynamic Investment and Product Market Rivalry: The Network Q Model
detail.abstract: We present a new dynamic model of corporate investment in imperfectly-competitive product markets, extending the neoclassical (Q) theory of capital to a multi-firm, multi-product, fullystructural model. Our model embeds a state-of-the-art hedonic demand system, endogenizes firms' markups and generalizes Tobin's Q to a matrix (or network) of product market spillovers, which captures how each firm's investment affects that of its rivals. We provide existence and uniqueness results along with exact, global analytical solutions for the Markov Perfect Equilibrium investment policies. We then take our model to the data for the universe of U.S. public companies and obtain five novel insights: 1) product market competition is a key force driving aggregate investment and capital allocation; 2) the persistence of firm's capital stocks increased over the past 25 years (i.e. capital became "stickier"); 3) monopoly rents account for a large, rising share of firms' value; 4) positive shocks to firms' cost of capital increase markups and concentration; 5) mergers consummated since 1995 have led to a modest decline in aggregate capital formation; at the firm-level the resulting increases in markups are highly heterogeneous.

title: Beyond biological timescales: a cascading framework for managing non-sustainable geological resources”
affiliations: University of Antwerp, University of Antwerp and Royal Belgium Institute of Natural Science - Geological Survey of Belgium

detail.title: Beyond biological timescales: a cascading framework for managing non-sustainable geological resources”
detail.abstract: Sustainable resource management has evolved significantly, yet the fundamental question of how to exploit geological resources sustainably remains unaddressed. This study returns to the sustainable development principles of Daly (1990), which provide physically grounded guidelines that, when properly interpreted, tested and extended, can inform geological resource management. We interpret Daly (1990) by making explicit the spatial specifications and volumetric criteria to account for the spectrum of geological renewability that a binary renewable/non-renewable classification overlooks. Before testing these interpreted conditions, we visualise regeneration-extraction relationships to reveal the mismatch between biological and geological resources. Daly’s principles assume regeneration at human timescales, while geological resources regenerate over planetary timescales. This mismatch creates a non-sustainable zone where most geological resources cluster permanently, making steady-state management physically impossible due to geophysical constraints. Rather than dismissing these principles, we propose gaining sustainability as a theoretical extension providing transitional pathways for resources that cannot achieve sustainable scale directly. These pathways create iterative movement toward the sustainable zone while demand reduces to levels geological systems can support. We operationalise this extension through a cascading methodology that systematically tests steady-state and pairing conditions before applying gaining sustainability pathways. Testing groundwater, deep geothermal energy, and CO₂ storage in the Campine Basin, Belgium, against these conditions demonstrates that geological resources exist along a renewability spectrum, revealing where each principle functions and where geological constraints make it inapplicable. The analysis and proposals in this study extend Daly (1990) to geological systems, bridging ecological economics and earth sciences.

title: Cost-Benefit Analysis of Contour Ridges as Rainwater Harvesting Technique for Climate Change Adaptation in Rangelands
affiliations: , The University of Jordan, Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg and Brandenburg University of Technology (BTU)

detail.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis of Contour Ridges as Rainwater Harvesting Technique for Climate Change Adaptation in Rangelands

declarations.funderStatement: This study was conducted within SAGE, a Global Climate Centre, funded by the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) [grant number 57592434].

detail.abstract: Restoration of degraded rangelands through rainwater harvesting (RWH) is an important intervention in arid and semi-arid regions to sustain rangeland productivity and ecosystem services. We conducted a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) to assess the economic viability of implementing contour ridges as an in situ RWH technique to restore degraded rangelands in Jordan. Jordan has vast pastoral areas and faces significant water scarcity, which is expected to intensify under climate change. We assessed the benefits of three essential ecosystem services: forage production, water availability, and prevention of soil erosion, and compared them with the costs of implementing and maintaining contour ridges and the initial forage loss incurred during the establishment of the forage shrubs. Our research design combined model-based biophysical simulation and economic valuation. For the biophysical simulation, we used the Global Range (G-Range) model to estimate the increase in forage production and the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model to estimate improvements in water availability and soil erosion prevention. The CBA was conducted across five distinct rangeland classes, differentiated by average annual rainfall, land slope, and soil organic carbon (SOC), which allowed us to cover 75% of Jordanian rangelands. Economic valuation was performed by monetizing benefits and costs to 2022 U.S. dollars over a 15-year project lifespan and by calculating the net present value (NPV) using an 8% discount rate, with sensitivity analyses at 5% and 12%. We considered two scenarios: the first incorporated the benefit of increased water availability from shallow groundwater aquifers, while the second excluded this benefit to reflect the current policy restrictions on groundwater extraction. The results of the CBA revealed positive NPVs in the first scenario and negative NPVs in the second scenario across all rangeland classes. These findings highlight the importance of the benefit of increased water availability when evaluating large-scale restoration projects.

title: Ethnic Diversity and Small-Scale Renewable Energy Penetration: Implications for Australian Neighborhoods
affiliations: Monash University, Monash University, Monash University - Department of Economics, Monash University and Fulbright School of Public Policy and Management, Fulbright University Vietnam

detail.title: Ethnic Diversity and Small-Scale Renewable Energy Penetration: Implications for Australian Neighborhoods
detail.abstract: This study examines how ethnic diversity influences the adoption of small-scale renewable energy technologies across Australian neighborhoods. Using postcode-level panel data from 2006–2021, we address endogeneity with multiple instrumental variable estimators, including mean-based IV and instrumental quantile regressions (IVQR). The results indicate that greater ethnic diversity reduces the uptake of solar photovoltaics (PVs) and solar water heaters but increases the adoption of air-source heat pumps, suggesting a substitution effect at the postcode level. Income-stratified analyses reveal marked heterogeneity across income groups. The findings highlight the role of socio- demographic composition in shaping renewable energy transitions and the need to account for ethnic diversity when designing adoption incentives at the community level.

title: Fiscal policy space and the unequal exchange of biodiversity loss in global agrifood trade
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Fiscal policy space and the unequal exchange of biodiversity loss in global agrifood trade
detail.abstract: Agricultural land-use change is the dominant driver of terrestrial biodiversity loss and is increasingly attributed to international agrifood trade. This study investigates the political-economic structures underpinning asymmetric flows of embedded biodiversity loss by integrating ecological unequal exchange (EUE) and post-Keynesian theoretical frameworks. We combine the ‘land-cover impacts on future extinction’ (LIFE) metric from the global environmental indicators of consumption (GEIC) dataset, GEIC’s underlying multi-regional input-output model GTAP 11, and a novel fiscal policy space index (FPSI), which captures national monetary sovereignty and position within the currency hierarchy, to analyse a global country-year panel. Results demonstrate that countries with greater fiscal policy space receive significantly higher monetary compensation for each land-use-driven extinction embodied in their agrifood exports. This higher compensation is associated with larger net imports of embodied land-use-driven extinctions, confirming a key mechanism of EUE. Mediation analysis reveals that monetary compensation partially transmits the effect of fiscal policy space on extinction outcomes, yet a strong direct effect remains, indicating additional structural transmission channels. These findings show that asymmetries in biodiversity loss are not merely a product of consumption patterns but are structured by global monetary and financial power relations. Consequently, territorially bounded conservation policies risk exacerbating leakage and inequity unless they engage with the international monetary and financial architectures that enable the externalisation of environmental burdens. This study advances EUE theory by explicitly linking fiscal policy space to land-use-driven species extinction outcomes and underscores the need for transformative governance of global food systems to address the nature crisis.

title: The symbiosis of sociometabolic regimes and capital-labour relations in late capitalism
affiliations: Roskilde University

detail.title: The symbiosis of sociometabolic regimes and capital-labour relations in late capitalism
detail.abstract: Explanations of material consumption trajectories primarily emphasise productive forces (such as technological change and shifts in energy carriers) while generally overlooking the role of social relations. This omission is particularly troublesome considering that shifts in social relations (toward decent work and community empowerment) are crucial for reducing inequality while mitigating environmental pressures. To overcome this limitation, I examine the relationship between capital-labour relations and material use trajectories in high-income economies, arguing that the two are symbiotic, that is, they are embedded in a mutually reinforcing, long-term interaction. I provide empirical substance to this framework by testing cointegration relationships between labour and material time series, characterised by bidirectional causality and unfolding across alternating periods of discontinuity and stability. On this basis, I show, through periodisation analysis, how labour-material symbiosis manifests through varying corporate and state strategies of subordinating labour and nature to the imperative of synchronising demand with growing productive capacity. This implies that the evolving interdependence of material use and social relations is key to understanding both the historical configurations and socioecological viability of capitalist economies.

title: Formation of international environmental agreements and payoffallocation
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - CERMSEM, Saint Petersburg State University, CNRS - Paris School of Economics and HEC Montreal - Department of Decision Sciences

detail.title: Formation of international environmental agreements and payoffallocation
detail.abstract: Dealing with climate change requires that all countries engage in costlyefforts to reduce their emissions. Reaching this objective has so far beenelusive because it is in the best interest of each country to let the othersdo the effort and benefit itself from a better environment. The presence ofnegative externalities and strategic behavior have made game theory anatural paradigm to design an international environmental agreement (IEA)that codifies what countries should do. Considering that countries aresovereign and no supranational entity can impose an agreement, a stream ofliterature adopted a noncooperative mode of play to the formation of anenvironmental coalition. On the other hand, as joint optimization of allcountries' payoff leads to the best outcome, cooperative games approach hasalso been proposed to share the cost of climate change. Both approaches havetheir pros and cons.In this paper, we propose a model of coalition formation that combines bothcooperative and noncooperative modes of play. Starting from any givencoalition, we implement a Markov process that shows sequentially whichcountries join or leave the coalition until reaching an absorbing state. Allpossible sequential scenarios are considered and an allocation to the playeris made taking into account individual rationality. An illustration withvulnerable and invulnerable countries to pollution is given.

title: Seven Modes: A Coordination Protocol for Human-AI Collaboration
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Seven Modes: A Coordination Protocol for Human-AI Collaboration
detail.abstract: Human-AI collaboration currently operates without shared reference. Users infer assistant state from context; assistants guess user intent from prompts. This interpretive variance produces friction, misalignment, and lost insight. This paper introduces State Architecture-a minimal coordination protocol that enables dynamic mode-switching without ceremony. Seven discrete cognitive states (Scan, Diagnose, Evaluate, Collapse, Execute, Validate, Chill) provide shared reference for human and machine, collapsing interpretive variance and enabling fluid transitions between exploration, construction, witnessing, and rest. The protocol is domain-general, requires no technical implementation, and emerges from observed coordination failures in existing systems. We provide full state definitions, transition logic, and case studies from active research collaboration. The protocol functions as a Common-Knowledge Coordination Signal, demonstrating that interpretive infrastructure can be engineered rather than inherited.

title: Robust Screening Mechanism under Ambiguity Theory and Application to Greenwashing

detail.title: Robust Screening Mechanism under Ambiguity Theory and Application to Greenwashing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare that there is no conflicting interest that has influenced the study

detail.abstract: We analyze a robust screening problem where a receiver seeks to accept high-quality senders and reject lowquality ones under Knightian uncertainty regarding the prior distribution of types. Departing from standard Bayesian models with common priors, we characterize the unique screening test that maximizes the receiver's worst-case expected payoff against an adversarial nature. The optimal mechanism partitions the state space into three distinct regions: a rejection zone, a trust zone of full acceptance, and an intermediate screening zone. We show that robustness necessitates intentional rationing-in the screening zone, the receiver must commit to accepting valid senders with a probability strictly less than one. This rationing is calibrated to render the worst-case adversarial sender indifferent between truth-telling and falsification. While the mechanism induces truthful reporting and eliminates direct falsification waste, it incurs a social cost in the form of allocative inefficiency. Comparative statics demonstrate that improvements in verification technology relax this rationing constraint, yielding a Pareto improvement for both the receiver and the sender.

title: Verifying Shareholders for Electronic Participation in General Meetings: Law and Case Studies in Baltic Listed Companies

detail.title: Verifying Shareholders for Electronic Participation in General Meetings: Law and Case Studies in Baltic Listed Companies
detail.abstract: To participate electronically in general meetings, shareholders and their representatives must be verified to confirm their identities. Electronic verification remains relevant today as virtual and hybrid meetings of shareholders are widespread across the globe. This article studies shareholders' electronic verification from the viewpoint of EU company law, domestic laws in the Baltic States, human rights instruments, data protection laws, and other sources; it focuses on three cases of companies from the Baltic States where shareholders were verified for electronic participation between 2021 and 2024. The three cases, from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, known for their digitalization efforts, are evaluated against the background of regional and domestic laws in those countries. The study reveals that verification spans multiple legal areas and is typically regulated by companies themselves. The paper concludes with recommendations for the more transparent and accessible electronic shareholder participation.

title: Bandwidth Saturation and Dimensional Collapse in Information-Processing Systems

detail.abstract: We establish a formal relationship between bandwidth constraints and system fragmentation across cognitive, organizational, and network domains. When the ratio of active information streams to parallel processing capacity exceeds a critical threshold (empirically ≈ 0.8), feasible configuration spaces undergo dimensional collapse, making fragmentation geometrically inevitable. This result demonstrates that bandwidth saturation produces structural necessity, not empirical contingency. The framework unifies phenomena from attentional narrowing to organizational silos under a common geometric principle.

title: Constraint Engineering: Equilibrium Shifts Through Interpretive Infrastructure
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Constraint Engineering: Equilibrium Shifts Through Interpretive Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Large-scale social change typically follows catastrophe not because trauma enlightens, but because catastrophe enforces constraint-collapsing interpretive variance, synchronizing perception, and eliminating exit options. This paper argues that catastrophe is merely a delivery mechanism for constraint, and that constraint itself can be engineered through non-traumatic infrastructure. Drawing on Common-Knowledge Coordination Signals (CKCS) and the Interpretation Layer State Variable (I_state), we demonstrate that equilibrium shifts in complex social systems follow the same mechanics as synthetic multi-agent coordination: variance collapse under shared reference. We formalize Constraint Engineering-the deliberate design of infrastructure that imposes credible, non-violent constraints to shift Nash equilibria before catastrophe does. The framework distinguishes between catastrophic constraint (externally imposed, high harm) and architectural constraint (internally embedded, auditable, reversible), showing that the latter can achieve equivalent equilibrium effects without trauma. We provide design primitives, falsification criteria, and implications for institutional reform, AI alignment, and social movements.

title: Can a Structured Governance Memory System (GMS) be Designed and Implemented to Enable Validator-Governed Protocols and DAOs to Make Better-Aligned Decisions that Avoid Unintended Consequences, Preserve Institutional Learning, and Increase Long-Term Resilience and Adaptability?

detail.title: Can a Structured Governance Memory System (GMS) be Designed and Implemented to Enable Validator-Governed Protocols and DAOs to Make Better-Aligned Decisions that Avoid Unintended Consequences, Preserve Institutional Learning, and Increase Long-Term Resilience and Adaptability?

declarations.ethicsApproval: All interviewed parties have given consent

detail.abstract:
The Governance Memory System (GMS) is a preventive decision-support architecture designed to reduce the accumulation of governance errors over time in validator-governed protocols and DAOs operating under decentralized coordination constraints. Surface-level metrics, such as voter turnout, token price, and proposal approval rates, fail to detect the latent power dynamics, procedural fatigue, and institutional amnesia that precede governance failure. 
Drawing on practitioner interviews and case studies from NEAR, Gitcoin, and Juno, this paper introduces a five-layer framework (Proposal Lifecycle Metadata, Outcome Review Anchors, Informal Power Mapping, Governance Health Index, Recurring Themes & Frictions) that tracks proposal lifecycles, anchors outcome reviews, maps informal power, and synthesizes feedback across governance cycles. Rather than treating governance as an episodic voting activity, GMS frames governance health as an adaptive process shaped by attention constraints, incentive alignment, and evolving mission objectives. 
Robust governance depends on a system's capacity to withstand stress, align outcomes with stated goals, and avoid collateral damage. It cannot solely rely on activity metrics. In decentralized environments where formal authority is limited and legitimacy must be continuously renewed, structured memory and adaptive feedback become infrastructural rather than optional.

title: Disintermediation Governance and Complementor Innovation: An Empirical Look at Amazon.com
affiliations: , Northwestern University, Kellogg School of Management and University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Disintermediation Governance and Complementor Innovation: An Empirical Look at Amazon.com
detail.abstract: This study investigates how the platform’s disintermediation governance policy, i.e., the policy that disciplines complementors and consumers circumventing the platform to transact directly, affects complementors’ product innovation and launching strategies. We leverage a change in the Communication Guideline on Amazon.com (i.e., the focal platform), which prohibits complementors (i.e., sellers) from sending external website links, telephone numbers, and email addresses to buyers in direct messaging, as a policy shock to Amazon complementors. By conducting a difference-in-differences analysis, we find that the governance policy significantly reduces product innovation on the focal platform among complementors with direct sales channels, as measured by the number of new products and the innovativeness of new products. These main effects are mitigated by complementor reputation on Amazon and complementor multihoming. Mechanism analyses show that complementors with direct sales channels increase the number of new products launched through those channels after the policy change, i.e., the switching effect. Moreover, complementors tend to strategically switch innovative and high-value products away from the focal platform while leaving less innovative but price-competitive products on it to attract Amazon consumers before diverting to their direct sales channels, i.e., the bait effect. Our results have implications for platform governance policies regarding disintermediation and its impact on complementor product innovation and launch strategies, both on and off the focal platform.

title: A Case-Based Evaluation of Quantum-Resistant Data Indexing Techniques for Blockchain Databases ​
affiliations: Virtual University of Pakistan, Virtual University of Pakistan and Virtual University of Pakistan

detail.title: A Case-Based Evaluation of Quantum-Resistant Data Indexing Techniques for Blockchain Databases ​
detail.abstract: Blockchain architectures make extensive use of authenticated indexing structures, such as the Merkle Tree, for integrity and efficient retrieval of the data. However, the advent of quantum computing; in particular, through the use of Shor's and Grover's algorithms, puts the classical cryptographic primitives (RSA, ECDSA, SHA-256) on which these systems are based at risk. While Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is a solution, its integration brings about large overheads in terms of computation and storage, which are not much explored in practical database environments. This research has a case-based assessment of quantum-resistant indexing techniques in a simulated healthcare environment. Using a hybrid experimental approach, this research compares a classical baseline (i.e. private Go-Ethereum network) against a custom Cryptographic Stress Test Engine modeling NIST standardized PQC algorithms: Dilithium3 (Lattice-based), XMSS (Stateful Hash-based), and SPHINCS+ (Stateless Hash-based). Experiments were performed on a dataset of 10,000 Electronic Health Records (EHR) using resource limited hardware (8GB RAM) to simulate a deployment in developing infrastructure. Empirical findings show a crucial "storage explosion" in designs that are resistant to quantum computing. While the classical ledger was only 1.2MB in size, the lattice-based Dilithium3 led to a 50x increase in storage requirement (62.8MB) and the stateless SPHINCS+ increased the storage requirement by 270x (325.9MB). In terms of indexing latency, Dilithium3 was a nice middle ground option (13.10s), while SPHINCS+ was computationally expensive (25.63s). The study concludes that stateless hash-based schemes provide long-term security for archive purposes.

This article, written by Dr. Ivo Pezzuto as part of the Forward Thinkers’ Talks Series, features an in-depth conversation with Martina Domenicali, Co-Founder and CRO of Lexroom, and examines a defining question reshaping Europe’s LegalTech landscape: can hyper-specialized, jurisdiction-native AI outperform horizontally scaled, general-purpose models in high-liability professions? In February 2026, the company surpassed €10 million in Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)—by curating over six million localized legal documents to build a data-first, deeply verifiable AI platform tailored to civil-law systems—an inflection point that places it among Europe’s fastest-scaling AI ventures.

The article investigates how depth-driven localization creates structural defensibility and how governance-by-design, source traceability, and human-in-the-loop workflows redefine professional practice. Evidence shows that precision and accountability—rather than generic LLM capability—drive sustained adoption, reflected in 93% retention and strong Net Revenue Retention.

Contrasted with Anthropic’s horizontal plugin model, Lexroom’s approach signals a broader theoretical shift: in regulated domains, competitive advantage stems from embedding AI within institutional authority and workflow infrastructure. The implication for scholars and executives is clear—durable AI leadership will be secured not by scale alone, but by context-embedded intelligence that transforms technology into a trusted professional backbone.

title: Can Psychological Heuristics Enable Long-Term Optimization? Evidence from Short-Form Video Recommendations

detail.abstract: Recommender systems optimized for short-term engagement often hurt long-term consumer satisfaction and retention. Yet optimizing long-term outcomes is challenging because such signals are sparse and noisy. We study short-form video platforms, where identifying videos that drive retention is particularly difficult because content is short and often passively consumed, making it hard to attribute long-term outcomes to any individual video interaction. We examine whether psychological heuristics can be helpful for long-term optimization in recommender systems. We propose the Attribution-Prediction-Optimization (APO) framework, which uses psychological heuristics to identify the most memorable moments within a session, trains a retention model on this structured signal, and incorporates retention predictions into a multi-objective ranking function. Among several candidate heuristics, the peak-end rule (Kahneman et al. 1993) performs best. We implement APO on Facebook Reels. Through a large-scale, long-term field experiment, APO significantly increases Daily Active Users and total sessions on Facebook Reels, with positive spillovers to the broader Facebook App, one of the largest gains observed on the platform and corresponding to approximately $555 million in annual revenue based on public revenue statistics. Conceptually, our work identifies a boundary condition for when behavioral insights improve machine learning (ML): Because ML relies on learning statistical patterns from big data, it naturally favors short-term objectives with high signal-to-noise ratios. In contrast, long-term objectives are sparse and noisy, and benefit from psychological structures to extract meaningful signals beyond what data alone can provide. Therefore, psychological and behavioral theory is particularly valuable for designing personalized AI systems that optimize long-term, rather than short-term, outcomes.

title: Higher Minimum Wages, Happier Customers? Quasi-experimental Evidence from Online Restaurant Ratings across the US
affiliations: Tilburg University and

detail.title: Higher Minimum Wages, Happier Customers? Quasi-experimental Evidence from Online Restaurant Ratings across the US
detail.abstract: This paper examines how increases in the minimum wage affect consumer perceptions of restaurants, as reflected in online ratings. Drawing on seven years of city-month panel data from TripAdvisor linked to detailed local minimum wage schedules, we exploit staggered minimum wage policy changes across contiguous counties in a difference-indifferences framework using novel counterfactual estimators and conventional two-way fixed effects. We find that, nationally, a minimum wage hike raises average city-level restaurant ratings and we further uncover heterogeneity across US regions. Mechanism tests show that operational adjustments, such as improved service quality through higher staff morale, are unlikely to explain these effects. Rather, market exits of lowrated establishments following higher labor costs plausibly constitute the main mechanism, implying a compositional effect. Overall, observed rating improvements largely reflect higher-quality survivors as opposed to uniform operational improvements. This is further corroborated by stronger rating increases in cities experiencing cash wage hikes-which exert more direct pressures on a restaurant's payroll-rather than minimum wage increases via tip credit hikes. Our findings bear implications for policy makers, consumers, and local businesses.

detail.abstract: For nearly a century, displacement predictions have consistently overestimated the labour market consequences of automation technologies. This paper proposes that the consistent directional error reflects a structural conflation: forecasters measure the speed of capability access and project displacement on a corresponding timescale, when the two dynamics are governed by different determinants and operate independently. The paper advances seven contributions. First, naming the unstated assumption dividing the displacement and complementarian traditions – AGI-R (artificial general intelligence as replacement) versus AGI-C (artificial general intelligence as coexistence) – transforms an implicit framing commitment into a testable empirical question, supported by five converging lines of evidence from biological neuroscience, philosophy of mind, deployment data, experimental studies, and meta-analysis. Second, the Access-Displacement Framework formalises the independence of capability access and economic displacement through two variables – the access gap (G_A) and the displacement gap (G_D) – with cross-generational evidence across five technology transitions spanning two centuries. Third, the Measurement Obsolescence Hypothesis documents accelerating degradation in Bureau of Labor Statistics benchmark data, with revisions escalating to 3.4 times the historical average in the absence of any declared recession. Fourth, the Sampling Residualisation Hypothesis identifies systematic survey nonresponse bias that disproportionately excludes workers who have adapted to artificial intelligence. Fifth, the Organisational Absorption Rate demonstrates that institutional integration capacity operates as a binding rate constraint regardless of technical capability – a distinction absent from thirty-five years of absorptive capacity research. Sixth, the Economic Forcing Function shows that the deceleration of Moore’s Law drives deployment toward hybrid architectures that structurally embed human participation. Seventh, the Hybrid Swarm Architecture describes the three-layer deployment topology these economic constraints produce. Each contribution is presented as a testable hypothesis with specified falsification conditions, not as a conclusion.

title: Structural Compression Theory: A Unified Information-Theoretic Account of Organizational Dysfunction, Creativity, and Substrate-Independent Selection Dynamics
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Structural Compression Theory: A Unified Information-Theoretic Account of Organizational Dysfunction, Creativity, and Substrate-Independent Selection Dynamics
detail.abstract:
Every system that coordinates at scale compresses information. It must. No alternative exists. The compression creates gaps between what the system sees and what is real. Selection fills those gaps—not with truth, but with whatever survives the selection environment. The result is drift: toward internal consistency, away from external accuracy. The sequence is as reliable as entropy and as avoidable.

The mechanism is substrate-independent. Multi-agent AI systems with no psychology, no career anxiety, and no culture exhibit the same dysfunction patterns as human organizations. Neural networks at 7 billion parameters exhibit the same compression-selection dynamics in their activation geometry. SEC filings show measurable entropy compression following formalization events. The physics does not care what the agents are made of. It cares how they coordinate.

The conventional explanations arrive on schedule after every institutional failure. Groupthink. Hubris. Toxic culture. Each is invoked with the confidence of a diagnosis and the precision of a horoscope. Each names the outcome and calls it the cause. Replace every executive with a humble one; the structure will produce the same outcome with nicer people in the meetings. Blaming groupthink for organizational failure is like blaming copper for electrical resistance. The copper is the medium. The resistance follows from the physics.

This monograph identifies the physics. Three theorems, a lemma, and five sufficient conditions—derived from rate-distortion theory, Crawford-Sobel strategic communication, and Kosko's forbidden interval theorem—formalize a single mechanism that produces both organizational dysfunction and creative emergence, distinguished only by the direction of the selection pressure. The same mechanism that produces organizational stupidity produces jazz. You cannot kill one without killing the other. They share a channel, a noise source, and a formal proof.

The monograph derives structural countermeasures from the formal framework: the Mirror (observation insulated from the selection environment it monitors), rigorous inquiry (validation from outside the frame being tested), ambient structure discovery (computational detection of patterns no human monitors), and Emergence (a constraint-based design paradigm where you write the constraints and the behavior writes itself). Sixteen appendix papers provide extended formal treatments. The framework generates falsifiable predictions across organizational behavior, AI alignment, cognitive science, and institutional design.

It does not ask to be believed. It asks to be tested.

detail.abstract:
This study challenges the universal “best time to post” heuristic by arguing that online communities exhibit distinct, measurable temporal signatures. We test whether the delay between information seeking (Google Search) and social engagement (Reddit) is random noise or a structural manifestation of collective cognitive processing. The goal is to explain why identical timing strategies succeed in some domains yet fail in others, and to replace one‑size‑fits‑all calendars with community‑specific timing that respects cognitive processing speeds and cultural rhythms. Methodologically, we conceptualize communities as damped harmonic oscillators, bridging physical signal processing with social theory. Using nine years of high‑frequency data from eight heterogeneous Reddit communities (N=125,432 posts) cross‑validated with contemporaneous Google Trends, we estimate dominant cycles via spectral analysis and quantify cross‑platform alignment with lead–lag correlation. A community‑level synchronization metric classifies behaviors and recovers incubation intervals. Robustness checks include windowing choices, detrending, surrogate tests for serial dependence, and sensitivity to overlap windows in Trends stitching.

Our findings uncover a three‑cluster typology shaped by community‑specific cognitive incubation: i) Synchronized communities show near‑instant coupling between search and discussion; ii) Phase‑shifted communities exhibit a consistent processing delay before conversation emerges; iii) Autonomous communities follow engagement rhythms largely independent of external search trends. The typology is stable across years and insensitive to reasonable preprocessing choices. Apparent “silence” frequently reflects a functional incubation gap rather than disinterest, explaining intra‑platform variance in content timing performance. While we rely on publicly available Reddit and Google Trends signals where platform policy shifts may introduce unobserved confounds, the lead–lag structure remains robust.

Theoretically, we extend Media Synchronicity Theory from medium‑level affordances to community‑level norms, motivating formal models of collective cognitive processing time. Practically, timing is redefined as a strategic variable rather than a universal constant. Managers should align cadence to community processing speed: real‑time automation for synchronized domains; “prime–wait–engage” sequences for phase‑shifted domains; and culture‑centric programming for autonomous communities. Socially, respecting incubation periods can improve discourse quality by reducing knee‑jerk posting and encouraging deliberation. We introduce community‑specific temporal signatures and a validated three‑cluster typology, reframing silence as a functional incubation gap and offering actionable guidance for campaign design and real‑time optimization.

title: Optimal Scheduling and Growth Bounds in Hierarchical Production under Rival Time

detail.title: Optimal Scheduling and Growth Bounds in Hierarchical Production under Rival Time
detail.abstract: Hierarchical production systems transform additive time allocations into multiplicative output gains. This architecture is pervasive in economic systems: organizational hierarchies, investment chains, large engineering and infrastructure projects all rely on the sequential construction of productive capacities, where each stage builds the productive means used by the next before final output can emerge. We model a finite acyclic hierarchy in which a single agent allocates time across sequential stages to maximize terminal output. Under convex effort technologies, optimal policies take the form of sequential cascades proceeding from upstream to downstream; under concave technologies, the optimum is interior but upstream priority is preserved. For any admissible allocation, if state technologies grow at most polynomially, terminal output is bounded by a polynomial in the time horizon; exponential growth is structurally impossible without productive feedback. Specializing to power technologies, we obtain a taxonomy indexed by state elasticity α and effort elasticity β, governing depth and organizational form. We then solve the linear case in closed form. The marginal condition for adding a stage yields a universal threshold converging to Euler's number e ≈ 2.718, reflecting the trade-off between multiplicative productivity gains and temporal dilution. Finally, we illustrate the framework with a calibrated application to industrial development pipelines. ⋆ Working paper.

title: The Cost of Cost Savings: Procurement Auctions and Moral Hazard in Drug Market

detail.title: The Cost of Cost Savings: Procurement Auctions and Moral Hazard in Drug Market
detail.abstract: Procurement contracts are central to big buyers like governments and major corporations, but their design can generate a moral hazard problem: winning firms with ex-ante secured quantity have incentives to cut costs by reducing quality ex-post. We examine this issue in an important healthcare setting: China's volume-based procurement (VBP) of generic drugs. Using regulatory filings and novel measures of patient retention and switching, we show that procured drugs face more supplier changes and lower patient retention, with patients more likely to switch to branded alternatives, consistent with quality reduction driven by moral hazard. To assess welfare implications, we estimate a structural demand model with unobserved heterogeneity and state dependence in drug choice. Our results indicate that procurement achieves ￥3.85 billion ($550 million) cost savings for statin drugs, while the decline of drug quality offsets 14.8% of cost savings. Together, these findings provide empirical evidence of supplier moral hazard in the healthcare procurement setting and underscore the importance of contract design to regulate quality.

title: Seeing Innovation: Green Plate Policy and Electric Vehicle Adoption
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School and University of Rochester

detail.title: Seeing Innovation: Green Plate Policy and Electric Vehicle Adoption
detail.abstract: Innovation such as electric vehicles is central to decarbonization and sustainability, but encouraging early adoption is costly. This study examines China's "green plate" policy, rolled out between 2016 and 2018, which uses green license plates to visually distinguish electric vehicles from gasoline vehicles. Applying difference-in-differences and synthetic control methods, we find that green plates increased EV sales by at least 6.3% (48,000) between late 2016 and 2018, an effect equivalent to 4.7 billion RMB in purchase subsidies. Heterogeneity analyses show stronger effects for EVs from traditional automakers and for premium models, and the policy also led to a marked rise in Baidu search intensity for "EV," consistent with informational salience and image signaling as key drivers of increasing adoption. These findings offer new insights into how symbolic, low-cost marketing levers and behavioral nudges can accelerate the diffusion of emerging technologies, offering a scalable alternative to monetary incentives.

title: Error Bounds for Assortment Optimization under Random Parameters Logit

detail.title: Error Bounds for Assortment Optimization under Random Parameters Logit
detail.abstract: An assortment optimization problem involves selecting a subset of products to maximize revenue. We present the assortment optimization problem under the mixed logit model demand (MXL-Assortment), where expected revenue involves an integral over a random parameter with no closed-form solution. Thus, only the solution from the MIP reformulation of the MXL-Assortment problem can be obtained. Using the Koksma-Hlawka inequality, we examine the upper bound of the margin of error between the approximated and true solutions (i.e., the approximation error). The bound consists of the product of variation and discrepancy. Variation depends on the support of the random variables, whereas discrepancy depends on the number of samples used (G) and the sampling strategies. Since computing variation is infeasible due to its dependency on the assortment, we derive an assortment-independent upper bound for the variation. For discrepancy, we compute an exact star-discrepancy value using a finite collection of sample subsets. In numerical experiments with 20 candidate products, the Halton sequence yields lower approximation error bounds than pseudo-random sampling and achieves comparable performance with roughly 80% fewer draws. Moreover, solutions yielded from Halton sequence are stable when G = 100 and G = 500, whereas pseudorandom sampling exhibits persistent inconsistency (about 0.2 products on average), despite their similar run times.

detail.title: Strategic Fit in Cloud Adoption: Business Strategy, Cloud Computing, and Operational Implication
detail.abstract: Problem definition: In the operations management (OM) community, cloud computing has been recognized as a transformative technology with the potential to enhance business processes. However, both survey evidence and industry feedback caution that cloud computing adoption does not guarantee value creation, and its realized benefits may vary substantially across firms. In this study, we investigate whether firms’ business strategy affects the adoption decision and operational implication of cloud computing technologies. Methodology/results: Using 10-K filings of U.S. public firms from 2005 to 2019, we develop a text-based measure of cloud computing adoption and a topic modeling measure of firms’ emphasis on a cost leadership strategy. Our empirical results suggest that firms with a stronger emphasis on a cost leadership strategy are more likely to adopt cloud computing and experience subsequent improvements in operational efficiency following cloud adoption. Further analysis indicates that reducing selling, general, and administrative (SG&A), research and development (R&D), and advertising expenses is an important mechanism through which cloud computing adoption enhances subsequent operational efficiency. Our results are robust to firm fixed effects, reverse causality tests using import tariff reduction shocks, instrumental variable approaches, matching methods such as propensity score matching and entropy balancing, and alternative measures of cloud computing adoption and cost leadership strategy. Managerial implications: Our study provides evidence that the adoption decision and operational implication of cloud computing depend critically on its alignment with firms’ business strategy. Firms pursuing cost leadership strategy should view cloud computing as a strategic tool for efficiency gains rather than merely an IT upgrade. They may leverage cloud computing technologies to optimize SG&A, R&D, and advertising processes. Cloud computing providers are also advised to develop cost-saving solutions that help firms achieve operational improvements.

title: Exact Rounding for Fair 𝑘-Median under Quasi-Convex Costs
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and Sharif University of Technology

detail.title: Exact Rounding for Fair 𝑘-Median under Quasi-Convex Costs
detail.abstract: We study a constrained variant of the classical k-median problem, where the goal is to select k facilities that minimize total client service cost. To promote fairness and balanced representation, we impose a partition matroid constraint: the facility set is divided into disjoint groups, and each group may contribute at most a specified number of facilities to the solution. To make this NP-complete problem tractable, we assume that, for each client, service costs are quasi-convex over an ordering of facilities-capturing scenarios like Hotelling's model, where cost increases with distance from a preferred option. Under this structure, we design an exact polynomial-time rounding algorithm that uses a novel coloring scheme to convert any optimal fractional LP solution into an integral one. Our approach iteratively selects two disjoint, well-balanced sets of red and blue clients and adjusts their assignments while preserving optimality. Our framework is flexible and extends to settings with facility opening costs and robust variants, where each client i must be assigned to their closest facilities and the goal is to minimize total multi-assignment cost. Experiments on healthcare facility placement in Alabama demonstrate strong empirical performance-even when quasi-convexity is violated-and quantify the trade-offs introduced by fairness constraints.

title: The Paulini Model of Legal Negotiation: A Structural Framework for Professional Negotiation

detail.title: The Paulini Model of Legal Negotiation: A Structural Framework for Professional Negotiation
detail.abstract:
Legal negotiations are often understood as a rational exchange of legal arguments. In practice, however, negotiations represent complex social interactions in which legal reasoning, psychological dynamics, and communicative processes interact simultaneously.

This paper introduces the Paulini Model of Legal Negotiation as a structural framework for understanding professional negotiation leadership. The model assumes that successful negotiation leadership emerges from the interaction of three central elements: legal clarity, psychological understanding, and the personal stability of the negotiator.

In addition, the paper develops the Clarity Chain of Negotiation, which describes the mechanism through which analytical clarity translates into leadership within negotiation conversations.

By integrating insights from negotiation theory, decision psychology, and communication research, the Paulini Model provides a conceptual framework for analyzing negotiation dynamics and for improving professional negotiation practice.

detail.title: Enhancing Airport Ground Movement Operations through Data: A Review with a Focus on Uncertainty Management
detail.abstract: Airport ground movement (AGM) is a critical component of air traffic management, connecting airside and airspace operations, with significant implications for efficiency, safety, and sustainability. With traffic volumes only set to grow in the coming years, the demand for robust decision support systems has intensified, particularly under the uncertainty introduced by human behaviour, environmental variability, and system complexity. While traditional optimisation methods rooted in operational research have provided strong foundations for routing and scheduling in AGM operations, they struggle to adapt to the dynamic and uncertain environments present in real-world problems. In parallel, advances in surveillance, guidance, and sensing technologies have enabled the widespread collection of historical and real-time data, creating opportunities for adaptive, data-driven approaches. This review traces the evolution of AGM decision support, contrasting knowledge-based and data-driven frameworks, evaluating their strengths and limitations in managing uncertainties. Particular emphasis is placed on human factors and uncertainty management, distinguishing between proactive planning approaches that incorporate uncertainty, and reactive approaches that respond to real-time disturbances. Future research opportunities and challenges lie in enhancing human-machine interaction, accelerating algorithmic speed for real-time decision making, and developing generalisable, data-augmented and explainable frameworks through interdisciplinary collaboration.

detail.abstract: We examine the impact of ex-ante target and acquirer information asymmetry (IA) measures on the performance of the combined post-merger firm. We propose a novel IA mismatch hypothesis that M&A deal and external parties can utilize which applies to simultaneous mismatches between the target and acquirer IA measured before the merger offer. This hypothesis examines how mismatches reflect the characteristics of the deal parties, and its influence on short-and long-run performance. We show that a highT-lowA IA combination (high or opaque target; low or transparent acquirer) is economically and significantly positively related to different measures of future longrun performance, but the opposite IA mismatch of lowT-highA (low or transparent target; high or opaque acquirer) has a negative impact. We attribute the former mismatch to IA capturing private target information that only low IA acquirers are better able to leverage due to greater transparency and better access to private information. We find that high IA acquirers "bite of more than they can chew", and perform poorly in the long run, no matter what the IA level of the target is.

detail.abstract:
Real-time delivery platforms have become central to modern logistics, healthcare, and on-demand services. These systems promise efficiency through live tracking, dynamic routing, and instantaneous dispatch. Yet despite widespread adoption of real-time visibility tools, many platforms continue to experience persistent failures, including missed service windows, workforce churn, rising costs, and inconsistent service reliability.

This paper argues that these failures are not primarily driven by insufficient data or technological limitations, but by misaligned incentive structures that distort participant behavior. Drawing on platform economics, behavioral operations, and incentive theory, the paper demonstrates why visibility alone cannot produce reliable outcomes.

The paper introduces a readiness- and feasibility-aware incentive framework that conditions evaluation and compensation on probabilistic task feasibility rather than rigid time-based thresholds. By treating incentives as a core architectural layer in real-time systems, this framework enables more stable, fair, and scalable platform performance under uncertainty.

This work contributes a conceptual systems-design perspective and outlines principles for integrating predictive modeling, incentive alignment, and behavioral feedback in large-scale operational platforms.

detail.abstract: For decades, leadership-whether in corporate, organizational, or equine contexts-has often relied on pressure-and-compliance models. Traditional paradigms assume that subordinates and teams will align through authority alone. Emerging research in psychophysiology suggests that such approaches may have measurable physiological and behavioral costs. In this research-informed essay, patterns of physiological and behavioral alignment across human-human and human-animal interactions are examined. Dyadic synchrony-rhythmic alignment of physiological and behavioral responses-appears as a biologically grounded pattern of relational alignment. Conceptual coherence provides a framework for understanding how trust, congruence, and engagement may influence coordination, learning, and adaptive interaction patterns. The Trust Card concept, an extension of the Epistemic Governance concept, is author’s own work and was developed independently. declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: No funding has been obtained for this work.

detail.abstract:
Institutions across sectors increasingly rely on complex systems - algorithmic, computational, and socio-technical, to inform consequential decisions, while lacking full access to or understanding of how those systems produce outcomes. Prevailing governance approaches emphasise transparency, explainability, performance metrics, or ethical principles. While important, these approaches do not fully resolve a central institutional problem: how decisions can be made legitimately and defended under conditions of partial knowledge.

This paper introduces epistemic governance as a distinct, domain-agnostic governance paradigm concerned with the institutional conditions under which confidence in system-mediated outcomes is established, bounded, and justified. Rather than governing computation directly, epistemic governance focuses on governing institutional action by structuring authority, oversight, and conditions of reliance when full transparency or certainty is unattainable.

As part of this framework, the paper conceptualises Trust Cards as one application of epistemic governance. Trust Cards are defined as institutional governance artefacts with a two-layer structure, separating internal epistemic assurance from external interpretive signalling. This separation enables institutions to preserve internal discretion while maintaining external legitimacy. The paper is conceptual in scope and intentionally does not specify operational implementations.

title: A Systematic Literature Review on Cost Structure Optimization and Financial Sustainability of a Dialysis Center: Break-Even and Sensitivity Analysis for Strategic Decision-Making
affiliations: , WORLD CITI COLLEGES and World Citi Colleges - Quezon City - Graduate School Department

detail.title: A Systematic Literature Review on Cost Structure Optimization and Financial Sustainability of a Dialysis Center: Break-Even and Sensitivity Analysis for Strategic Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Hemodialysis facilities have high fixed costs that are challenging to change. Along with expenses for water systems, dialysis machines, and facility fees, these are primarily distributed to employees as pay. Other significant variable cost during every dialysis session is dialyzers, bloodlines, concentrates, disposables, medicines, and utilities. In different low-and middleincome countries, variable expenses take a greater proportion of total expenditures depending on the mode of acquisition of commodities, the stability of the supply chain, and the manner of payment. Due to this, any small variations in the quantity of patients attended to will affect the amount of money significantly. The break-even point is calculated by the contribution of each session to the fixed costs coverage and the possibility of the dialysis center to maximize its capacity. The dialysis facilities can enhance the profitability as they can reduce the amount of treatment expenses per case by increasing their number of treatments since fixed costs are distributed among the sessions. Even slight changes in the fixed costs imply that a facility must offer much more sessions to meet such costs. The breakeven point may also rise in case the variable costs rise. Annual per-patient hemodialysis expenses in countries with low and middleincome are quite diverse with some financial barriers to the centers without the government cover or subsidies. Consequently, free-standing dialysis centers in effect have an increased risk of financial loss because of low safety margins that make it easy to make losses, restrain investments and reduce the services even though the break-even point is close to, not to mention difficulties in the nature of irregular cash flow and late payment. Therefore, dialysis centers must pay an emphasis on the fact that their resources are to be managed successfully, there has to be enough cash on hand, and they have to receive supplies. Additional studies are required to effortlessly identify the effectiveness of standard costing and scenario planning among various types of centers and systems of payment.

title: The Erosion of Global Disease Research Investment in a Fragmenting World: National Egocentrism, Rising Military Expenditure, War Impacts on Health, and Migration Pressures (2020-2026)
affiliations: University of Yaounde I - Faculty of Science

detail.title: The Erosion of Global Disease Research Investment in a Fragmenting World: National Egocentrism, Rising Military Expenditure, War Impacts on Health, and Migration Pressures (2020-2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no funding.

detail.abstract: Between 2020 and March 2026, the global community experienced unprecedented and compounding stresses to its collective security architecture. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed that infectious diseases constitute borderless threats capable of destabilizing societies simultaneously. Yet paradoxically, the post-pandemic period has been characterized by escalating military expendituredriven by wars in Ukraine (2022-present), Gaza (2023-present), Sudan, and most critically, a major regional war erupting in the Middle East in March 2026-while investment in disease-related research has declined following its emergency surge. Concurrently, conflict-induced displacement has reached record levels, and direct war impacts have destroyed health infrastructure across multiple regions, creating new disease vulnerabilities. The March 2026 escalation has now disrupted global health supply chains, suspended operations at WHO's Dubai emergency logistics hub, and created new disease surveillance gaps across 16 directly affected countries. In this Review, we argue that national egocentrism, securitized responses to migration and conflict, and escalating geopolitical rivalries have collectively reshaped global investment priorities in ways that fundamentally undermine long-term human security. By integrating trends in military spending, war-related health destruction, disease burden, population mobility, and research funding, we highlight a growing structural vulnerability: the systematic underinvestment in health research despite clear evidence that pathogens-amplified by conflict and displacement-represent the most universal and recurrent threat to humanity. Drawing lessons from COVID-19 and multiple concurrent wars, we call for renewed global solidarity and sustained, predictable investment in health research, commensurate with military spending, as the only viable foundation for resilient global security.

title: Predicting Adverse Selection in High-Frequency Cryptocurrency Markets Using Gradient Boosting
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati and Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati

detail.title: Predicting Adverse Selection in High-Frequency Cryptocurrency Markets Using Gradient Boosting
detail.abstract: We predict adverse selection in high-frequency cryptocurrency markets using gradient boosting (LightGBM) trained on 31,081,463 second-level observations of BTC/USDT perpetual futures on Bybit, spanning February 1, 2025 through February 16, 2026 (381 raw daily files). Our toxicity label (tox_A) identifies seconds where strong directional order flow is followed by sustained price continuation over a five-second horizon, constructed using adaptive rolling quantile thresholds calibrated to a one-hour lookback windowa regime-aware design that accommodates the substantial variation in toxicity rates observed across the sample, ranging from 0.081% in September 2025 to 0.795% in February 2025. The model is estimated in a strict walk-forward regime: the first 21 days serve as the initial training window, with 360 out-of-sample evaluation days beginning February 22, 2025, eliminating any forward-looking bias. The composite TailScore-the product of the classifier's predicted toxicity probability and its predicted 99th-percentile absolute price move-jointly captures the likelihood and severity of an adverse selection event. At a 0.1% gate, the TailScore achieves monthly ROC-AUC between 0.668 and 0.921 across the full out-of-sample period. The central result is that flagging the top 0.1% of TailScore-ranked seconds reduces CVaR99 by 2.33%-a reduction 25.85 times greater than an equal-sized random gate. This efficiency ratio persists across all tested gate widths from 0.1% to 5.0%, decaying from 25.85x to 3.50x as the gate widens, consistent with the model's signal being concentrated in the extreme upper tail of the score distribution. Monthly evaluation confirms robustness: efficiency ranges from 15.18x to 34.88x across all 13 evaluation months, with no month falling below the random gating benchmark. An ablation study isolates the contribution of the TailScore against a pure GBM classifier and a VPIN proxy. The classifier alone achieves an efficiency of 2.11x and the VPIN proxy 0.30x-the latter falling below the random benchmark-at identical gate rates. The gap between TailScore (25.85x) and classifier alone (2.11x) demonstrates that the severity component is the dominant driver of CVaR reduction: predicting that a toxic event will occur is insufficient; predicting how large the move will be is what determines whether the gate concentrates on the seconds that matter most for tail risk.

title: Understanding Patient Experience in Mental Health Counseling and Support Services (2021–2026): A Patient-Centered and Administrative Analysis of Effective and Ineffective Care Approaches

detail.title: Understanding Patient Experience in Mental Health Counseling and Support Services (2021–2026): A Patient-Centered and Administrative Analysis of Effective and Ineffective Care Approaches

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Mental health services have expanded significantly over the past decade, yet many individuals seeking counseling, therapy, or behavioral support report dissatisfaction with the care they receive. Research published between 2021 and 2026 increasingly emphasizes that patient outcomes in mental health care are influenced not only by clinical treatment methods but also by relational dynamics, communication practices, and system design. This paper reviews contemporary literature examining how patients experience interactions with counselors, therapists, and support specialists, and which care approaches contribute to improved engagement and treatment outcomes. Particular attention is given to therapeutic alliance, shared decision-making, cultural responsiveness, trauma-informed practice, and measurement-based care. The analysis also explores the administrative implications of these findings, emphasizing how organizational structures and clinical workflows shape the patient experience. By examining both empirical research and real-world case observations, this paper argues that effective mental health support requires adaptable, patient-centered communication and system-level accountability mechanisms that align care delivery with patient needs.

title: Accounting for imperfect displacement in life cycle assessment for refurbishing and remanufacturing operations
affiliations: University of Padua, Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, INSEAD and INSEAD

detail.title: Accounting for imperfect displacement in life cycle assessment for refurbishing and remanufacturing operations
detail.abstract: Refurbishing and remanufacturing are often championed for their potential to reduce environmental impacts, yet their true benefits remain a subject of debate. A primary challenge is imperfect displacement-where refurbished/remanufactured units do not fully substitute for new products-leading to rebound effects that can offset environmental gains. Recent Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) research has begun to address this through a displacement rate (DR), which compares the quantity of new products displaced to the quantity of refurbished/remanufactured products supplied to the market. However, practical approaches to estimating realistic DRs remain limited, with most studies resorting to subjective assumptions. This article shows how to endogenize DR by using an established modeling approach from the Operations Management literature. This involves modeling firm and customer decisions and estimating DR as a function of cost, market, and operational parameters. We propose that companies must verify whether this market-driven DR exceeds the 'break-even' DR-the threshold required for a circular strategy to achieve net environmental savings, as calculated through LCA. We demonstrate these notions through a case study in the electronics industry. Our results highlight that, for products with usedominated impacts, companies must strategically select their target markets, as geography significantly influences both break-even and market-driven displacement. Overall, we provide scholars and practitioners with an interdisciplinary framework to evaluate the environmental benefits of refurbishing/remanufacturing strategies. This framework offers a practical calculation with feasible data requirements, enabling firms to simulate prospective scenarios and identify actionable levers to influence displacement with both environmental sustainability and profitability in mind.

title: Refugee Return
affiliations: , European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Ifo Institute and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Refugee Return

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite rising refugee numbers worldwide, refugees’ return decisions remain poorly understood. Prior work examines either intentions or realized return, but not both. We fielded a ten-wave panel of Ukrainian refugees, linking prewar home municipalities to geocoded conflict and territorial control data and eliciting war expectations. Intentions strongly predict behavior: by 2025, 42% of those planning to return soon in 2022 had returned, versus 1% of those planning to settle abroad. Increasing conflict in the home municipality reduces return there but barely affects return to Ukraine overall. More pessimistic war expectations explain 21% of the decline in return intentions.

title: Energy Markets at War: The Effect of the Russian Invasion of Ukraine on Refinery Margins
affiliations: and German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf - Department of Economics

detail.title: Energy Markets at War: The Effect of the Russian Invasion of Ukraine on Refinery Margins

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the effect of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 on refinery margins, i.e. the difference between wholesale prices for road fuels (gasoline and diesel) and oil prices in Europe and Germany in particular. Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, wholesale road fuel prices net of taxes rose by more than 50 cents per liter, whereas crude oil prices increased by only about 30 cents per liter. Using a difference-in-differences framework, we compare refinery margins in Germany with those on the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp (ARA) spot market, which serves as a European benchmark price. The results indicate that refinery margins in Germany increased by approximately 5–6 cents per liter relative to the ARA region after the invasion. We attribute this differential primarily to Germany’s strong dependence on Russian Ural crude oil imports and to the presence of regional market power among German refineries. We further document substantial heterogeneity in treatment effects across both time and regions. In addition, the invasion was associated with a significant decline in fuel demand, with gasoline consumption falling by about 13% and diesel consumption by approximately 9%.

title: Climate-Resilient Built Environments in Scotland: Planning Systems, Adaptation Strategies, and Implications for Medium-Sized Cities

detail.title: Climate-Resilient Built Environments in Scotland: Planning Systems, Adaptation Strategies, and Implications for Medium-Sized Cities
