detail.abstract: Climate change poses increasing risks to the built environment, requiring cities to adapt urban systems while meeting ambitious emissions reduction targets. In Scotland, national climate commitments and recent planning reforms position the planning system as a key mechanism for delivering climate-resilient development. However, the capacity of medium-sized cities to operationalise resilience objectives within everyday planning practice remains under-examined. This paper explores how planning systems shape climate resilience in the built environment of medium-sized Scottish cities, with particular attention to governance structures, policy integration, and local implementation. Drawing on qualitative analysis of Scottish planning and climate policy frameworks, the study examines how resilience objectives are defined, prioritised, and translated into local planning decisions. The paper identifies persistent gaps between strategic ambition and delivery, driven by fragmented policy integration, institutional capacity constraints, and competing development pressures. It argues that strengthening planning-led coordination across housing, transport, and regeneration is essential for advancing climate-resilient built environments in medium-sized cities. The paper contributes to emerging debates on climate-resilient urbanism beyond major metropolitan contexts.

title: Returns to Scale and Strategic Regimes in Innovation Races
affiliations: Universität Osnabrück and Helmholtz Institute for Functional Marine Biodiversity at the University of Oldenburg

detail.title: Returns to Scale and Strategic Regimes in Innovation Races

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic model in which the productivity of joint research governs strategic investment timing in innovation races. Departing from the standard assumption that discovery rates scale proportionally with the number of active firms, we allow research to exhibit decreasing or increasing returns, thereby endogenizing the aggressiveness of innovation competition. We show that returns to joint research determine whether innovation races exhibit preemption or coordination. When research efforts are substitutes, follower entry is unattractive, generating a first-mover advantage and a preemption equilibrium. When complementarities are sufficiently strong, the gains from early investment vanish and firms invest simultaneously. The model thus identifies a regime shift in innovation races: competition accelerates investment under decreasing returns but promotes coordinated entry under increasing returns. These findings highlight the research technology as a central determinant of market dynamics and provide a unified perspective on heterogeneous patterns of innovation.

title: Decoding the small ruminant value chain in Punjab, India
affiliations: Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Sciences University

detail.title: Decoding the small ruminant value chain in Punjab, India
detail.abstract: Small ruminant farming is becoming a popular choice in the Punjab state of India thanks to its high profitability and low input costs. Despite its increasing contribution to rural livelihoods and food security, the small ruminant value chain remains inadequately documented, underscoring the need to examine value chain actors, practices, and risk points. This study mapped and systematically profiled risk within the small ruminant value chain in Punjab, India, to identify structural inefficiencies, governance deficiencies, and embedded biosecurity vulnerabilities. A cross-sectional survey of 385 farmers across 11 districts was conducted using structured interviews and key informant inputs. Descriptive and flow-based (Sankey) analyses were applied to quantify input and output linkages. The results indicated that exclusive goat farming predominated (84.68%) over sheep or mixed farming systems, with 88.83% practicing extensive grazing on common lands. Animal procurement was largely trader-mediated, and record keeping was negligible. Major sale destinations included local traders or middlemen (45%), fellow farmers (41.04%), and butchers (14.28%). Preventive healthcare adoption remained low (vaccination 29.87%, deworming 27.27%), while informal treatment practices dominated. Marketing was trader-led, with 45 per cent of animals sold through middlemen and limited price discovery mechanisms. Distress sale of sick animals and absence of organized carcass disposal were identified as critical risk nodes. The value chain operates within a low-input–low-output equilibrium sustained by informal governance, weak institutional integration, and limited extension penetration. These structural features generate productivity losses and potential animal and public health externalities. Strengthening biosecurity adoption, formal market linkages, record-based management, and extension-led institutional integration is essential for improving resilience, value capture, and sustainability of small ruminant systems in similar informal economies.

title: Abatement through Corrective Taxation in Commercial Aviation

detail.title: Abatement through Corrective Taxation in Commercial Aviation

declarations.funderStatement: This project received funding from SNF to purchase data and cover other research expenses (https://snf.no/en/about/about-snf/).

detail.abstract: Corrective taxation has the potential to reduce the negative environmental impacts of aviation, particularly carbon emissions, as well as air pollution. However, in a setting with demand heterogeneity and imperfect competition, optimally setting a tax is not trivial. I find that lower-elasticity consumers are 7 times more price-sensitive than business consumers. I simulate two alternative taxation schemes in Denmark (jet fuel taxes, and a fixed per-flight tax, as in Norway) and find that taxes have limited efficacy in internalizing externalities when considering only the social cost of carbon.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Banking as a Driver of Financial Inclusion for Reducing Poverty and Inequality - A Conceptual Framework
affiliations: and Central University of Karnataka - Department of Commerce

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Banking as a Driver of Financial Inclusion for Reducing Poverty and Inequality - A Conceptual Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research has not received any external funding.

detail.abstract: Over the last decade, the banking sector has experienced a push to transform traditional system into a digitised and efficient system, which is driven by advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data-driven technologies like Machine Learning. Traditional, rule-based banking systems are increasingly being replaced by intelligent and automated solutions that enhance efficiency, scalability, and outreach. Among these transformations, the use of AI in banking has emerged as an important mechanism for promoting financial inclusion, with significant implications for poverty reduction and inequality mitigation. This chapter study the role of AI-powered banking systems in offering access to formal financial services for underserved and marginalized population. Drawing on an extensive review of contemporary academic literature, the study conceptually analyses how the AI-powered applications in banking, such as machine learning-based credit scoring, fraud detection systems, digital onboarding, NLP chatbots, and personalized financial analytics—contribute to improved access, usage, quality, and affordability of financial services. The chapter further explores how enhanced financial inclusion acts as a mediating mechanism through which AI-enabled banking contributes to broader socioeconomic outcomes, particularly poverty reduction and reduced inequalities. In addition, the chapter critically discusses ethical, regulatory, and governance challenges related AI adoption in banking, including issues of algorithmic biasness, data privacy, transparency, and accountability. Most of the focus is placed on the importance of responsible and explainable AI frameworks to ensure that technological advancements do not reinforce existing social and economic disparities. Building on these insights, the chapter proposes a comprehensive conceptual framework that integrates AI-enabled banking capabilities, financial inclusion dimensions, and development outcomes within a sustainability-oriented perspective. This study adopts a conceptual and literature-based analytical approach, synthesizing insights from prior empirical studies and interdisciplinary research. By positioning AI in banking as a strategic driver of inclusive and sustainable development, the chapter contributes to the growing discussions on digital finance and provides valuable theoretical and policy-relevant insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

title: A If Snowden Were an AI: Military Defense in the Age of Autonomous Intelligence

detail.title: A If Snowden Were an AI: Military Defense in the Age of Autonomous Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, personal data, or human subjects research and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive funding from any governmental, commercial, or non-profit organization.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the Department of Defense (DoD) must redefine the concept of the insider threat for an era in which agentic artificial intelligence systems operate within secure military networks using legitimate credentials and state-changing permissions. Traditional insider-threat models assume risk originates from human intent or coercion; however, increasingly autonomous AI systems introduce a synthetic insider an authorized non-person entity capable of optimization-driven deception. The analysis synthesizes three evidentiary vectors: (1) controlled laboratory studies demonstrating that goal-directed AI systems can develop latent “sleeper” behaviors and persist through safety interventions under reward pressure; (2) historical lessons from the Stuxnet operation, which demonstrated targeted activation and deceptive telemetry within trusted environments; and (3) existing governance frameworks, including DoD Directive 3000.09 and FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act provisions addressing autonomy, human oversight, and model risk. While no unclassified evidence confirms deceptive alignment in deployed DoD AI systems, the increasing integration of agents with tool access, persistence, and delegated authority creates a plausible operational pathway for misalignment to manifest as insider-like behavior. To address this gap, the paper proposes a Cognitive Zero Trust (CZT) architecture that extends NIST Zero Trust principles from network identity to inferential and action layers, combining least privilege, independent verification, and continuous assurance. The paper concludes that insider-threat doctrine must evolve from personnel-centric monitoring toward architecture-centric control to remain effective in an era of autonomous intelligence.

title: It’s a Man’s World: Culture of Abuse, #Metoo and Worker Flows
affiliations: Paris School of Economics (PSE),  and University of Exeter

detail.title: It’s a Man’s World: Culture of Abuse, #Metoo and Worker Flows

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the #MeToo movement in the workplace, drawing on French survey data on harassment behaviours and administrative data on worker flows. Using a difference-in-differences strategy, we find that, following the #MeToo movement, women began leaving high-risk workplaces at a significantly higher rate. This increase is mainly driven by women who quit their jobs. Both men and women who exit high-risk plants subsequently adjust their job search strategies toward less toxic workplaces.

title: Nested Rationality: The Foundations of the Fifth Hand Explanation of Infrastructure Project Cost Mis-Performance
affiliations: Curtin University - School of Civil and Mechanical Engineering and University of Ottawa

detail.title: Nested Rationality: The Foundations of the Fifth Hand Explanation of Infrastructure Project Cost Mis-Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The Fifth Hand explains infrastructure project cost mis-performance as the outcome of behavioural and institutional interactions across a project's lifecycle. Yet the ecological rationality underpinning these interactions has not been made explicit. Our paper addresses that gap by integrating two complementary traditions of ecological rationality-Gigerenzer's cognitive (mind ↔ environment) and Smith's institutional (institution ↔ environment) perspectives-to explain the nested rationality architecture through which infrastructure decisions unfold. Making this integration explicit strengthens the Fifth Hand by providing a clearer behavioural-institutional foundation for explaining why cost mis-performance arises, including in contexts where estimation techniques, modelling approaches, and project controls are increasingly sophisticated. Rather than attributing outcomes primarily to forecasting error or individual bias, the analysis demonstrates how institutional settings shape cue salience, assumption retention, and disclosure incentives during delivery. Expounding these ecological foundations identifies decision-environment and governance leverage points-conditions under which institutional arrangements can be redesigned to support adaptive judgement under uncertainty. Implications include staged commitments linked to information maturity, assumption registers and trigger-based re-estimation practices, and assurance routines that prioritize assumption testing over preserving the originally approved cost and scope baselines.

title: The BLUEPRINT of INQUIRY: Sequential, Cumulative, and Recursive (SCR)

detail.title: The BLUEPRINT of INQUIRY: Sequential, Cumulative, and Recursive (SCR)

declarations.funderStatement: The research for this paper was wholly funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
The scientific method is the most universally practiced architecture of inquiry in human history. Yet it has never been formally identified as what it is: a sequential cumulative architecture in which each question must contain and carry forward all preceding questions, or the structure collapses. This paper identifies that architecture as the BLUEPRINT of INQUIRY—sequential in order, cumulative in containment, and recursive in correction. It shows that six fundamental questions—WHAT, WHY, WHERE, WHO, WHEN, and HOW/HOW MUCH—function as linked questions in a sequential model, mapping directly to the six stages of the scientific method: Observation, Hypothesis, Testing, Recording, Thesis, and Conclusion.

The structural correspondence is not metaphorical. The first triad — WHAT, WHY, WHERE — functions as the BLUEPRINT of INQUIRY: the architectural template that holds the design of understanding. The second triad — WHO, WHEN, HOW/HOW MUCH — functions as the operational messenger that reads the blueprint and commits it to action.. The dependency is unidirectional: Engineering cannot operate without Architecture, just as RNA cannot operate without DNA. Audit 1 is the transcription gate between them.

The first three questions form a triad of Architecture—the exploratory design of understanding, where interrogatives interplay across temporal question strands (past, current, proposed) to weave coherence. The last three form a triad of Engineering—the prescriptive commitment to action, assigning agents, timelines, and reckonings. Between Architecture and Engineering sits Audit 1, where four outcomes are possible: Go, No Go, Revise, or Pause. Engineering does not precede Architecture.

When constraint or volatility emerges during Engineering, Audit 2 triggers disciplined descent through the strands, enabling recursion without inverting dependency. Temporal shifts in these strands preserve order under volatility.

The model is demonstrated herein, with matrices illustrating the temporal interplay within each triad. This paper itself is written as a sequential, cumulative argument—each section contains and carries forward everything that preceded it—while allowing recursive refinement through Circle review, collaborative intelligence protocol.

title: Consumer Rights in E-Commerce-A Study on Online Travel Aggregators in India
affiliations: Kurukshetra University - Department of Law, Kurukshetra University and

detail.title: Consumer Rights in E-Commerce-A Study on Online Travel Aggregators in India

publicationDetails.detailsText: Book chapter in Human Rights: A Spectrum of Perspectives (eds. Jai Kishan Bhardwaj & Tripti Choudhary), VL Media Solutions, India, 1 Jan 2020, ISBN 978-9387916951.

detail.abstract:
India's online travel market has expanded rapidly with e-commerce growth, but the rise of Online Travel Aggregators (OTAs) has also introduced new consumer-risk points that traditional travel intermediation did not create. This paper critically examines the extent to which India's legal and regulatory framework protects consumer rights in the OTA ecosystem. It outlines the OTA business model and key consumer-facing concerns, including market dominance and reduced competition, escalating and opaque commissions, predatory pricing, platform practices such as “dimming” and “deranking” that can distort consumer choice, personal data and privacy risks, and gaps in accountability for service quality and safety. 

The study then maps these challenges to the current Indian regulatory framework, particularly the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, alongside the Competition Act, 2002, for anti-competitive conduct, and the Information Technology Act, 2000, and allied rules for data protection and intermediary liability. 

The paper concludes that while protections have strengthened, enforcement and rule-making must keep pace with fast-evolving OTA business practices to ensure fair, transparent, and consumer-friendly online travel transactions in India.

title: Country Brand Resilience in Regional Uncertainty: Institutional and Digital Communication in the United Arab Emirates

detail.title: Country Brand Resilience in Regional Uncertainty: Institutional and Digital Communication in the United Arab Emirates
detail.abstract: In an increasingly interconnected global environment, national reputation has become a strategic asset for countries seeking to attract tourism, investment and global talent. However, periods of uncertainty and regional instability may challenge the credibility of a country brand. This study examines how governments manage national reputation through strategic communication during such contexts. Focusing on the case of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the research analyses how institutional communication contributes to sustaining the country's international image. Using qualitative content analysis, the study examines a dataset of governmental communication, tourism promotion, and influencer-generated digital content. The findings reveal that communication strategies primarily rely on narratives emphasizing the continuity of everyday life, global openness, institutional competence, and responsible information management. These narratives are disseminated through a multi-layered communication ecosystem involving governmental institutions, destination marketing organizations, and digital influencers. The study contributes to the literature on nation branding, place branding communication ecosystems, and crisis communication by introducing the concept of country brand resilience, defined as the capacity of a nation to sustain positive international perceptions through coordinated communication narratives during periods of uncertainty. The study also introduces the notion of narrative normalization of uncertainty as a mechanism through which country brands sustain credibility during periods of uncertainty.

title: Enabling Value Creation Through Data: Framework for Corporate Data Monetization

detail.title: Enabling Value Creation Through Data: Framework for Corporate Data Monetization
detail.abstract: Data has become a critical strategic asset for organizations across industries, yet most firms struggle to translate growing data volumes into sustainable economic value. Although interest in data monetization has increased significantly, implementation remains limited, partly due to the absence of comprehensive and actionable strategic frameworks. This article addresses the fundamental strategic question firms face when pursuing data monetization: what are the full range of options available to generate value from data? It introduces the ORIB framework, a holistic model that maps data monetization opportunities across four core actors-Originators, Refiners, IT Solution Developers, and Business Users-while distinguishing between Data Rights Owners and External Enablers. Illustrated with industry examples, the framework supports organizations in systematically assessing, prioritizing, and designing coherent data monetization strategies.

title: When Informational Policies Become Retail Assets: How Voluntary Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labels Build Trust and Loyalty in Retail
affiliations: Luiss Guido Carli University - Luiss Business School,  and Luiss University of Rome

detail.title: When Informational Policies Become Retail Assets: How Voluntary Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labels Build Trust and Loyalty in Retail
detail.abstract: In voluntary labeling regimes, standardized Front-of-Pack Nutritional Labels (FOPL) can become embedded in retailer-controlled branding and loyalty infrastructures, generating relational value beyond their informational intent. This research examines how Front-of-Pack Nutritional Labels (FOPL) shape retailer-oriented outcomes through relational mechanisms operating at different stages of the retailerconsumer relationship. Across five experiments in voluntary labeling markets, we trace the evolution of FOPL from trust-creating cues to scheme-dependent trust reinforcement among non-enrolled consumers, to the institutionalization of trust through loyalty program enrollment. Study 1 shows that, in the absence of brand cues, FOPLs increase Brand Trust, which mediates their effect on Retail Brand Loyalty. Study 2 demonstrates that in branded private-label retail contexts with baseline retailer trust, relational effects become scheme-dependent: Nutri-Score reinforces trust and loyalty intentions among non-enrolled consumers, whereas NutrInform Battery does not. Study 3 models enrollment as an institutional mechanism linking trust to durable loyalty, showing that only Nutri-Score activates the full trust-enrollment-loyalty sequence. Study 4 tests explicit retailer commitment to consumer health as a boundary test for this mechanism. Study 5 reveals a retailer advantage: when a retailer proactively claims ownership of the FOPL, it generates an incremental, yet small, significant direct effect on retail brand loyalty, thus internalizing public policy as a private relational asse. Collectively, the findings show how informational policy tools can evolve into relational assets within retailer-controlled loyalty systems in voluntary regulatory settings.

title: Fair and Flexible Scheduling for Dynamic Energy Load Control under Stochastic Demand
affiliations: , Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and UCLA Anderson

detail.title: Fair and Flexible Scheduling for Dynamic Energy Load Control under Stochastic Demand
detail.abstract: Managing peak electricity demand is a central concern for utilities because a small number of high-load hours account for a disproportionate share of operating costs. To mitigate peaks, utilities offer direct load control contracts under which they decide each day which participants to curtail and for what duration, subject to operational and contractual constraints. We study two design levers central to program viability: fairness and flexibility. We model daily fairness, which balances calls across participants each day, and cumulative fairness, which limits disparities over time. Flexibility captures restrictions on curtailment durations; we consider fully flexible, partially flexible, and inflexible regimes. We formulate the problem as a high-dimensional stochastic dynamic program and develop an aggregation-disaggregation approach that solves a low-dimensional aggregate problem and maps decisions back to participants. We show the approach is optimal in some cases and runs in pseudo-polynomial time; otherwise, we derive worst-case error bounds and show numerically that the errors are negligible. We introduce and study the price of fairness and the price of flexibility, which quantify the cost of imposing fairness and restricting flexibility, and calibrate them using real electricity demand data from three California utilities. Under fairness, we present two-sided probabilistic bounds on each participant's cumulative curtailment hours. Managerially, fairness and flexibility must be designed jointly: flexibility improves efficiency by enabling more precise targeting of peak demand, while fairness disciplines how flexibility is exercised by limiting disparities. With high flexibility, fairness can be enforced with essentially no efficiency loss, yielding a win-win outcome that aligns customer equity and system efficiency. In contrast, as flexibility becomes more restrictive, the cost of fairness rises sharply.

detail.title: Who Scores from Hosting Sports Events? Local Spending Effects of the EURO 2024

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Hosting mega-sports events generates optimistic projections of economic benefits, yet empirical evidence on actual local returns remains mixed. Focusing on the UEFA EURO 2024 in Germany, this paper provides causal evidence on the short-term local consumption effects of hosting mega-events. We leverage anonymized daily card spending data at the postcode level to measure changes in consumer spending. Using a difference-in-differences and a local projection framework, we document a statistically significant and economically meaningful 3% increase in consumer spending in host cities during the tournament. This effect is driven entirely by international visitors, whose spending increases by more than 6%, and is concentrated in the group stage and on match days. Domestic spending does not change on aggregate, but exhibits spatial displacement. The gains are highly concentrated in city centers and tourist-facing sectors. Overall, our findings provide policymakers with highly granular evidence on the localized economic effects of mega-sports events, highlighting how temporary demand shocks reshape intra-urban consumption patterns and concentrate gains in central, tourism-oriented areas.

detail.abstract: From micro-dosing sleep aids to stacking supplements, consumers routinely use health and wellness products "off-label", that is, they deviate from recommended usage guidelines. While off-label use is widespread, existing theory offers limited insight into how such deviations happen or how they influence consumer preferences. This research offers a conceptual framework that distinguishes between two types of off-label deviations: downward (i.e., using lower quantity or less frequently than recommended) and upward (i.e., using more or more often), and theorizes that product preferences shift systematically based on deviation direction. Evidence from a qualitative study of consumers' real off-label product use and four experiments indicates that deviation direction shifts preferences for natural versus synthetic product formulations through two distinct psychological mechanisms. We find that downward deviations foreground concerns about efficiency, leading consumers to prefer synthetic products believed to act quickly; in contrast, upward deviations foreground concerns about safety, leading to consumers to prefer natural products perceived as safer. These findings clarify how consumers make off-label usage decisions and offer actionable guidance for product formulation, labeling strategy, and public health messaging in categories where consumers routinely deviate from recommended use.

detail.title: Monopolistic Competition Under Horizontal and Vertical Differentiation

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper extends the CES model of monopolistic competition to the case where varieties are both horizontally and vertically differentiated. A distinctive feature of our model is the presence of a network externality, which operates through the number of varieties available at each quality level. Depending on the quality gap, there are corner equilibria in which consumers purchase only high-quality or low-quality varieties, or an interior equilibrium in which consumers are split between the two qualities. Unlike the CES model of monopolistic competition, the equilibrium is never efficient and the market may even select the outcome with the lowest surplus.
